title: I've been coding trading algorithms for ~7 years. Here's what backtests won't tell you.
author: Independent-Cry-3686
selftext:
I've been coding trading algorithms for \~7 years. Here's what backtests won't tell you.

I'm a developer and I've been building and running my own trading algos for about 7 years. (I wrote all of this myself in my own words and only used AI to translate.) I've tried a lot of indicators and strategies, all coded myself. Every time a backtest came back with promising numbers I got excited. I ran some live for years, and there were stretches where they did really well.

But here's the trap. Backtesting (and even paper trading) can make everything look great. The backtest code, yours or someone else's, might be simulating fills too optimistically. It might be ignoring fees and slippage. And it's never exactly the same as running against live prices. So being stuck in a bit of an illusion is almost unavoidable.

The technical/code side is where it actually gets hard.

A bot that runs a strategy and places orders has to be technically very solid. You need to really understand how the exchange you're connected to (Binance, etc.) works, and the edge cases need to already be handled. Writing a bot that "just works" on day one is basically impossible. Unexpected problems will show up, guaranteed.

A few things that bite people:

**Decimals.** Most languages, and most AI when it writes the code, reach for float64. Don't. Use a proper decimal library, otherwise lost/extra fractional values eventually cost you.

**Synchronization.** The big one. You send an order over the API and it can error, or respond late. Your system thinks it failed but the exchange actually filled it. Orders get partially filled. Half gets cancelled. The exchange can close a position on its own without telling you. There are a lot of ways your system and the exchange drift out of sync, and you have to design for every one of them. If you're coding with AI, you have to explicitly tell your model about this; it won't handle it by default.

**Rate limits.** Use websockets for price data. Don't burn API calls you don't need, and stay inside the exchange's limits.

One thing I genuinely believe: the strategy and the code should guide you, but you make the final call. Sometimes what's going on globally tells you not to buy even when your strategy says buy. Your own knowledge and experience have to stay in the loop.

I wanted to share two things with you here: an honest, experience-based writeup, and the tool I eventually ended up building off the back of it.

After all these years I ended up building a tool that automates the algorithm and code side of all this — the decimal handling, the sync, the rate limits and more. I'm the builder: it's at [algomax.ai](https://algomax.ai) and there's a free tier. But mostly I'd like to hear how the rest of you handle the sync and partial-fill problems.
